1. Introduction to Programming
Acomputer program consists of a series of instructions that a computer processes to perform
the required operation. Instructions in the computer programs are written using programming
languages . A computer program consists of three basic parts:
1. The instructions to be executed
2. The order in which the instructions are to executed
3. The data required to perform the instructions (input)
1.1 Program Development Cycle
Program development cycle has the following phases:
1.Analyze/Deﬁne the problem: The programmer has to analyze the problem thoroughly to
know about the scope of the problem.
2.Task analysis: Next, the programmer has to develop various solutions to the solve the prob-
lem. From these solutions, the optimum solution is chosen to solve the problem comfortably.
3.Develop algorithm: After selecting the optimum solution, algorithm is developed to depict
the logic of the selected solution.
4.Test algorithm for accuracy: Algorithm has to be checked for accuracy before it is converted
to actual code. This will enable the programmer to identify major logical errors at an earlier
stage of program development.
5.Coding: After testing the algorithm, actual code is prepared in a preferred programming
language.
6.Test and debug the program: The compiler of the programming languages test the program
for syntax errors. Also, the results obtained from the program is compared with the results
calculated manually using a number of sample input data.
7.Documentation: After all the errors in the program are corrected, the programmer has to
support the program with sufﬁcient document, so that the users can understand how to operate
the program.
8.Implementation: In this phase, the program is installed on the end user’s machine. This
phase can be considered as the ﬁnal testing, because only after using the program, the user

1.2 Algorithm
An algorithm is deﬁned as a ﬁnite sequence of explicit instructions that, when provided with a set
of input values, produces an output and then terminates. An algorithm should have the following
properties:
• There must be no ambiguity in any instruction
• There should not be any uncertainty about which instruction should be executed next
• The execution of the algorithm should conclude after a ﬁnite number of steps
• Algorithms must be general enough to deal with any circumstances

Rule of Generation: Avoid hand-hacking; write programs to write programs when
you can.
Using code generators can increase reliability and reduce errors as hand-hacking programs can
lead to delays and mistakes. Generated code is often cheaper and more reliable than hand-written
code. It’s beneﬁcial to use code generators when they raise the level of abstraction, meaning the
generator’s language is simpler than the generated code and no further hand-hacking is required.
Rule of Optimization: Prototype before polishing. Get it working before you opti-
mize it.
Prototyping ﬁrst is recommended as it saves time and effort, prevents investing too much time in
marginal gains, and avoids premature optimization which can lead to complex code and decreased
performance. The tradition in the Unix world is to prototype, then polish, and make it work
before optimizing it. Kent Beck’s "Make it run, then make it right, then make it fast" approach
reinforces the idea of focusing on functionality ﬁrst and optimizing later. Using prototyping to
learn which features you don’t have to implement helps optimization for performance; you don’t
have to optimize what you don’t write. The most powerful optimization tool in existence may be
the delete key.
Rule of Diversity: Distrust all claims for “one true way”.
The Unix tradition values openness and ﬂexibility in software design and avoids "one true way"
approaches. It recognizes the limitations of software tools and designers and embraces multiple
languages, open and extensible systems, and customization options to accommodate different uses.
This approach reﬂects a healthy mistrust of rigid, closed software and acknowledges the importance
of communication and integration with the rest of the world.
Rule of Extensibility: Design for the future, because it will be here sooner than you
think.
In software design, it is important to avoid assuming that your designs are ﬁnal. It is wise to leave
room for growth and extension, and to design protocols and ﬁle formats to be self-describing and
extensible. When designing code, it should be organized in a way that allows for future development
and new features to be added easily without having to scrap the existing architecture. This requires
making the joints ﬂexible and leaving comments for future developers to understand and build upon.
This approach ensures that code remains usable and maintainable over time.
1.2 History of Unix
Ken Thompson, who was a scientist at Bell Laboratories, invented Unix in 1969. Unix was one
of the ﬁrst systems that allowed programmers to create programs directly on the computer. Many
skilled programmers have contributed to its development over the years who were frustrated with
the limitations of other operating systems. So they helped make Unix even better.
The original Unix operating system was written in assembler, and the applications in a mix
of assembler and an interpreted language called B. But B was not powerful enough for systems
programming, so Dennis Ritchie added data types and structures to it and crated a new language C
1971. In 1973 Thompson and Ritchie ﬁnally succeeded in rewriting Unix in C.
The University of California, Berkeley became a key hub for Unix development. In 1980, the
Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) chose Berkeley Unix as a platform to
implement its TCP/IP protocol stack on the V AX under Unix, due to its available and unencumbered
source code. This led to the merging of ARPANET and Unix cultures.
1.3 Comparing Unix with MacOs 13
In 1981, Microsoft bought QDOS and in the same year, Sun Microsystems founders built a
Unix machine with built-in networking capability, which resulted in the founding of the workstation
industry. In 1982, C became the systems-programming language of choice, which drove machine
assemblers almost completely out of use. By the early 1990s, C and C++ dominated systems and
application programming.
In 1985, Richard Stallman issued the GNU manifesto and launched the Free Software Founda-
tion. The same year, the originators of the X window system released it as source code without
royalties or restrictions, which made it a safe neutral area for collaboration between Unix vendors
and became Unix’s graphics engine.
In 1987, the ﬁrst version of the GNU C compiler appeared, and by the end of the year, the
core of the GNU toolset was falling into place. In August 1991, Linus Torvalds announced the
Linux project. The Linux and BSD development efforts were native to the internet and relied on
distributed development and Larry Wall’s patch(1) tool.
The mass-marketing of the internet in 1993 increased the pool of potential developers and
lowered the transaction costs of distributed development. By late 1993, Linux had both internet
capability and X, and the entire GNU toolkit had been hosted on it from the beginning, providing
high-quality development tools. Linux collected twenty years of open-source software that had
previously been scattered across a dozen different proprietary Unix platforms, resulting in a
production-ready operating system.
1.3 Comparing Unix with MacOs
The Macintosh operating system was ﬁrst developed by Apple in the 1980s and was inspired by
GUIs developed by Xerox’s Palo Alto Research Center. The operating system has gone through
several design transitions, including the ability to multitask multiple applications and a shift from
Motorala’s 68000 processors to PowerPC processors. The Mac Interface Guidelines specify how
applications should look and behave, which has inﬂuenced the culture of Mac users. MacOS
applications are designed to have a clean separation between the application engine and GUI
interface, and MacOS ﬁles have both a data fork and a resource fork for storing user-deﬁnable ﬁle
attributes. MacOS has weak internal boundaries and a cooperative, not pre-emptive, multitasking
system. The Macintosh was designed for nontechnical end users, leading to a low tolerance for
interface complexity. The Macintosh has a strong hobbyist culture with a tradition of small tools,
shareware, and user-supported software. The Classic MacOS has been replaced by MacOS X,
which incorporates MacOS facilities into a Unix infrastructure derived from the Berkeley tradition.
1.4 Windows
Windows NT is a computer operating system developed by Microsoft that is used for high-end
personal and server use. It has several variants that can be considered the same. All Microsoft
operating systems since Windows ME in 2000 have been NT-based. NT is descended from VMS
and has some of its characteristics. However, NT has grown by accretion and lacks a unifying
metaphor like Unix. The GUI facilities coexist uneasily with the weak, remnant command-line
interface inherited from DOS and VMS. Most programs cannot be scripted, and there are no generic
tools at all. Documents and databases cannot be read or edited without special-purpose programs.
System and user conﬁguration data are centralized in a central properties registry rather than being
scattered through numerous dotﬁles and system data ﬁles as in Unix. NT systems on the Internet
are notoriously vulnerable to worms, viruses, defacements, and cracks of all kinds. NT suffers from
a chronic conﬁguration problem called "DLL hell."

1.5 Linux
Linux is a type of open-source Unix operating system that was created by Linus Torvalds in 1991.

Many developers and activists in the Linux community aim to win a substantial share of

1.6 Documentation
There are two types of documentation programs: WYSIWYG and markup-centered. WYSIWYG
programs, like desktop-publishing and word processing software, have graphical user interfaces
where what you type appears directly on the screen in a format similar to the ﬁnal printed version.
Markup-centered systems, on the other hand, use ﬂat text with visible control tags that don’t
resemble the ﬁnal output. To create the ﬁnal output, the marked-up text must be fed into a formatter
program. The marked-up text can be edited using a regular text editor.
Markup-centered documentation systems often have a macro facility. Users can create macros
that are expanded by text substitution into sequences of built-in markup requests. Macros usually
add structural features, such as declaring section headings, to the markup language.

1.7 Open Source Software
The rules of open-source development are:
1.Let the source be open. Have no secrets. Make the code and the process that produces it
public. Encourage third-party peer review. Make sure that others can modify and redistribute
the code freely. Grow the co-developer community as big as you can.
2.Release early, release often. A rapid release tempo means quick and effective feedback.
When each incremental release is small, changing course in response to real-world feedback
is easier.
Just make sure your ﬁrst release builds, runs, and demonstrates promise. Usually, an initial
version of an open-source program demonstrates promise by doing at least some portion
of its ﬁnal job, sufﬁcient to show that the initiator can actually continue the project. For
example, an initial version of a word processor might support typing in text and displaying it
on the screen.
3.Reward contribution with praise. If you can’t give your co-developers material rewards,
give psychological ones. Even if you can, remember that people will often work harder for
reputation than they would for gold.

Anything that is not public domain has a copyright, which means the people who made it own it.

authors are can be tricky for software made by many people, so licenses are important. They allow
certain uses of the code that wouldn’t be allowed under copyright law, and can protect users from
the copyright holders.
In proprietary software, licenses protect the copyright holder and give a few rights to users. The
copyright holder is very important, and the exact terms of the license usually don’t matter much.
But in open-source software, the license terms are very important because they determine what
users can and can’t do. The copyright holder doesn’t matter as much, and often the project leader
or sponsoring organization holds the copyright. Some open-source projects assign copyright to the
Free Software Foundation to help defend open source.
1.7.2 Portability
Software portability refers to the ability of software to be easily moved or adapted to different
hardware and software platforms without requiring signiﬁcant changes to the code. When software
is portable, it can run on multiple platforms with minimal effort, which can be beneﬁcial for
software developers and users alike.
1.7.3 Portability and Choice of Language
C Portability
The core C language is very portable, meaning it can be used on different computer platforms with
minimal changes to the code. The GNU C compiler is a commonly used implementation of C
for Unix systems, both open-source and proprietary. It can also be used on Windows and classic
MacOS, but is not widely used there because it lacks certain features for the native graphical user
interface (GUI). However, C can have portability issues with inter-process communication (IPC),
threads, and GUI interfaces.
Shell Portability
Shell-script portability is not very good, meaning shell scripts are not always guaranteed to work on
different platforms without modiﬁcation. The problem with shell scripts is not the shell itself, but
rather the other commands and ﬁlters that are used within the script. These are often not portable
and may not be available on all target machines. It is possible to overcome this problem with a lot
of effort, as is done with autoconf tools. However, this is difﬁcult and not always practical. Because
of this portability problem, many programmers have moved away from using shell scripts for heavy
programming and have instead turned to second-generation scripting languages like Perl, Python,
and Tcl.
Perl Portability
Perl has good portability. But, Perl scripts often require add-on libraries from CPAN (the Compre-
hensive Perl Archive Network) which are not guaranteed to be present with every Perl implementa-
tion.
Python Portability
Python has excellent portability. Stock Python has a much richer standard library than does Perl
and no equivalent of CPAN for programmers to rely on.

1.8 Best Practices for Working with Open-Source Developers
1.8.1 Good Patching Practice
Most people become involved in open-source software by writing patches for other people’s
software before releasing projects of their own. When submitting patches, it’s important to keep in
mind the following points.
Do send patches, don’t send whole archives or ﬁles.
If the change includes a new ﬁle that doesn’t exist in the code, then of course the whole ﬁle must
be sent. But if an already-existing ﬁle is modiﬁed, don’t send the whole ﬁle. Send a diffinstead;
speciﬁcally, send the output of the diff(1) command run to compare the baseline distributed version
against the modiﬁed version.
Send patches against the current version of the code.
The person submitting a patch is responsible for keeping track of the source code and sending
the maintainer a small patch that clearly communicates what they want to be done with the main
codebase. This entails sending a patch against the latest version.
Don’t include patches for generated ﬁles.
Sometimes, when changes are made to a ﬁle in a software project, the tool or application being
used may automatically regenerate or recreate that ﬁle when the project is rebuilt. Patches for these
ﬁles should not be included.
Do include documentation with your patch.
When changes are made to a software project that affect the way users interact with it, it’s important
to also update the relevant documentation ﬁles, such as man pages. It’s not safe to assume that
the person receiving the patch will be willing to document the changes for, or that they will be
comfortable with undocumented features.
Properly documenting your changes shows consideration for the person who will be reviewing
and applying your patch. Ultimately, taking the time to document changes shows that the person
care about the users of the software and their experience with it.
Do include an explanation with your patch.
It is important for a patch to include cover notes that explain the reasoning behind why the patch is
necessary or beneﬁcial. These explanations are intended for the maintainer who will be reviewing
and applying the patch, rather than for the end-users of the software.
Do include useful comments in your code.
The person in charge of maintaining the software project wants to be sure that they understand
the changes made before adding them to the project.Good comments in code help the maintainer
understand it. Bad comments don’t.
Don’t take it personally if your patch is rejected
There are various reasons why a patch may not be accepted, and most of them do not reﬂect on the
person who submitted it. It’s important to keep in mind that many maintainers are under signiﬁcant
time constraints, and have to be careful about what changes they accept to avoid causing issues
with the project code.

1.10 Free Software vs Open Source software
Free software and open source software are two different concepts, even though they are sometimes
used interchangeably.
Free software refers to software that is licensed in a way that allows users to run, copy, distribute,
study, change and improve the software. This means that the source code of the software is available,
and users can modify and distribute it as they wish. The focus of free software is on user freedom,
and the concept is closely associated with the Free Software Foundation and the GNU project.
Open source software, on the other hand, refers to software whose source code is made
available to the public, but the focus is not necessarily on user freedom. The open source deﬁnition
emphasizes the practical beneﬁts of making software source code available, such as allowing
developers to collaborate and improve the software. The concept of open source is often associated
with the Open Source Initiative and the Linux operating system.
In short, free software is about user freedom, while open source software is about transparency
and collaboration.

2.2 File Ownership and Permission
All ﬁles and directories in Unix have a set of access permissions which determine who has what
type of access to them.
2.2.1 Different types of Permissions
Three types of permissions for a ﬁle in Unix are
•Read : Permission to view the contents of a ﬁle.
•Write : Permission to modify or delete a ﬁle.
•Execute : Permission to run a ﬁle as a program.
Three types of permissions for a directory in Unix are
•Read : Permission to list the contents of a directory.
•Write : Permission to add or remove ﬁles from a directory.
•Execute : Permission to list information about ﬁles in a directory.
2.2.2 Owners and Groups
Unix has three levels of permission - owner ,group , and other - to enable collaboration among
users. The group permission allows a set of users to access a ﬁle, such as a team of programmers
working on a project. Each ﬁle has an owner and a group, with the owner usually being the user
who created the ﬁle. Users can belong to multiple groups and assign different groups to their ﬁles
to provide access to speciﬁc users.
The ownership and permissions of ﬁles in a directory can be displayed with the command

2.3 Shell
The Unix system is logically divided into two different areas: the kernel and the utilities. The kernel
is the heart of the Unix system and resides in the computer’s memory from the time the computer is
turned on and booted until the time it is shut down. The various tools and utilities that make up the
full Unix system reside on the computer’s disk and are only brought into memory and executed
as requested. Virtually every Unix command is a utility. The shell is also a utility program and is
loaded into memory for execution as part of the login sequence.
2.3.1 Types of Shell
The Bourne Shell
The Bourne shell (sh) is the preferred shell for shell programming because of its compactness and
speed. It was written by Steve Bourne at AT&T Bell Labs. A Bourne shell drawback is that it lacks
features for interactive use, such as the ability to recall previous commands (history). The Bourne
26 Chapter 2. File System and Basic Commands
shell also lacks built-in arithmetic and logical expression handling. In Bourne shell, the default
prompt for root user is #and for non-root user it is $.
The C Shell (csh)
It is written by Bill Joy at the University of California at Berkeley. It added features for interactive
use, such as aliases and command history. It includes features, such as built-in arithmetic and a
C-like expression syntax. In C shell, the default prompt for root user is #and for non-root user it is
%.
The Korn Shell (ksh)
Korn shell written by David Korn at AT&T Bell Labs. It supports everything in the Bourne shell. It
has interactive features as in C Shell. It also Includes convenient programming features like built-in
arithmetic and C-like arrays, functions, and string-manipulation facilities. It is faster than the C
shell. In Korn shell, the default prompt for root user is #and for non-root user it is $.
The GNU Bourne Again Shell (bash)
bash is compatible to the Bourne shell. It incorporates useful features from the Korn and C shells.
In bash, arrow keys are automatically mapped for command recall and editing. Default prompt for
Root user is bash-x.xx# (Where x.xx indicates the shell version number). Default prompt for a
non-root user is bash-x.xx$ (Where x.xx indicates the shell version number).
2.3.2 Responsibilities of a Shell
Program Execution
The shell is responsible for the execution of all programs requested from the terminal. For a shell,
each line has a basic format
programname arguments
The shell uses special characters to determine where the program name starts and ends, and where
each argument starts and ends. These characters are collectively called whitespace characters, and
are the space character, the horizontal tab character, and the end-of-line character, known more
formally as the newline character. Multiple occurrences of whitespace characters are ignored by the
shell. The shell scans this command line and determines the name of the program to be executed
and what arguments to pass to the program.
Variable and Filename Substitution
Shell allows to assign values to variables. Whenever a variable preceded by a dollar sign is speciﬁed
on the command line, the shell substitutes the value assigned to the variable.
The shell also performs ﬁlename substitution on the command line. In fact, the shell scans the
command line looking for ﬁlename substitution characters * , ? , or [...] before determining the
name of the program to execute and its arguments. For example,
echo *. pdf
prints the names of ﬁles in the directory with extension .pdf.
I/O Redirection
Shell scans each entered command line for occurrences of the special redirection characters
• < (input redirection character)
•> (output redirection character). When redirecting output to a ﬁle using >, the output ﬁle will
be created - or overwritten if it already exists
•» (output redirection character). Redirecting output to a ﬁle using » will append the output to
the ﬁle if it already exists.
For example,

echo hello world > sample .txt
will redirect the output of echo command (i.e. "hello world") to the ﬁle sample.txt.
Hooking up a Pipeline
Like redirection characters, shell scans the command line for the pipe character |. For each match, it
connects the standard output from the preceding command to the standard input of the subsequent
one, then initiates execution of both programs. For example,
who | wc -l
When the whocommand executes, it produces a list of who’s logged in and writes the results to
standard output. When the wccommand executes, it recognizes that no ﬁlename was speciﬁed and
counts the lines on standard input, unaware that standard input is coming from the output of the who
command.
Environment Control
The shell provides certain commands to customize environment, which includes home directory,
the characters that the shell displays to prompt to type in a command, and a list of the directories to
be searched whenever a program is to be executed.
Interpreted Programming Language
The shell has its own built-in programming language. This language is interpreted, meaning that the
shell analyzes each statement as encountered, then executes any valid commands found.Programs
developed in interpreted programming languages are typically easier to debug and modify than
compiled ones. However, they can take longer to execute than their compiled equivalents. The
shell programming language provides features which are available in most other programming
languages. It has looping constructs, decision-making statements, variables, and functions, and is
procedure-oriented.

3. Job Control
3.1 Introduction
The shell provides facilities for controlling jobs directly from the command line. A job is any
command or command sequence in the shell. At times, commands that require a few minutes or
longer to complete may need to be run. In those cases, users have to wait for the command to ﬁnish
executing before they can proceed further, unless they execute the command in the background . A
command or command sequence can be put into background by appending it with the ampersand
character &. For example:
1sleep 30
Running this program in the background will result in
$ ./ trial .sh &
[1] 10681
$
When a command is started in the background (that is, with &), the shell prints out the job number
inside brackets ([]) as well as the process ID. This means that the command will no longer tie up
the terminal, and the user can then proceed with other work. When a job ﬁnishes, the shell prints
the message
[n] + Done sequence
where nis the job number of the ﬁnished job, and sequence is the text of the command sequence
used to create the job.
The jobs command is used to print the status of jobs that haven’t completed.
$ jobs
[1] Running ./ trial .sh &
[2] - Running ./ trial2 .sh &
[3]+ Running ./ trial3 .sh &
The + and - after the job number mark the current and previous jobs, respectively. The current job
is the job most recently sent to the background, and the previous job is the next- to-the-last job sent
to the background.

4.1 Regular Expression
Deﬁnition 4.1. A regular expression is a pattern consisting of a sequence of characters that
is matched against a text.
Regular expression is made up of atoms andoperators .
• Atom - Speciﬁes what we are looking for and where in the text the match is to be made
•Operator - Combines atoms into complex expressions. Regular expressions are constructed

4.1.1 Atoms
Atoms can be
1. Single Character
2. Dot
3. Class
4. Anchor
5. Back Reference
Single Character
If a regular expression is made up of a single character, pattern looks for that single character in the
text. If the character does not appear in the text, pattern match is unsuccessful.
Dot
Dot matches any single character except the new line character. It can be combined with other
atoms. For example, a.means any pair of characters where ﬁrst character is a. So it matches aa,ab,

Class deﬁnes a set of characters. Class matches only one single character that can be any of the
characters in the set. For example [ABC] can match either AorBorC. A range of characters can be
speciﬁed by a dash. For example [A-Z] means any character from AtoZ. A^inside square bracket
indicates negation. For example [^ABC] means any character other than A,B,C. Back slash (\) is
used as escape character. For example if we want to match for -inside class, we need to give the

Anchors are special characters that anchor regular expressions to particular places in a string.
Anchors are of four types
1.^Beginning of the line

3. \< - Match the empty string at the beginning of word
4. \> - Match the empty string at the end of word.
The caret ˆ and the dollar sign $ are meta-characters that respectively match the empty string at
the beginning and end of a line.
Back Reference
Back reference is a mechanism for referring saved text while matching a pattern. It is made possible
by nine save buffers \1, \2 . . . \9
4.1.2 Operators
Operators combine atoms. Operators can be grouped into ﬁve categories.
1. Sequence
2. Alternation
3. Repetition
4. Group
5. Save
Sequence

Repetition
Repetition operator is a set of escaped braces \{ \}, that contains two numbers separated by a
comma. {M,N} means The preceding item is matched at least M times or at most N times. {N}
means the preceding item is matched exactly N times. {N, } means the preceding item is matched
at least N times.
Some other repetition operators are
• ? - preceding item is optional and will be matched at most once.
• * - preceding item will be matched zero or more times.

Short Circuit Logical Operators
Java provides two short circuit logical operators &&and ||. The truth table for these operators are
same as the truth table for &and | respectively. But the difference is that, &&and || will not bother to
evaluate the right-hand operand when the outcome of the expression can be determined by the left
operand alone. Hence, if the left operand of &&isfalse , it will not evaluate the right operand since
the result will be false regardless of the right operand. Similarly, if the left operand of || is true, it
will not evaluate the right operand since the result will be true regardless of the right operand. This
helps when the right-hand operand depends on the value of the left operands in order to function
properly. For example, consider the following code segment:
1if (a != 0 && b / a > 10)
In this code segment using &in place of &&may result in a runtime exception, because &will evaluate
both left and right operands. Hence if ais zero, b/awill cause a runtime exception. When &&is
used, there is no risk of causing a run-time exception when ais zero, since it will not evaluate the
second operand if the ﬁrst operand is false .

2.1 Object-Oriented Programming
In Object-oriented programming a program is developed around its data (called objects) and a
set of well-deﬁned interfaces that operate on those data. The characteristics of object oriented
programming are
2.1.1 Abstraction
Abstraction is a process by which internal details of an application are hidden from outside world.
2.1.2 Encapsulation
Encapsulation is the mechanism with which data and code that manipulates the data are bound
together. Encapsidation keeps both data and code safe from outside interference and misuse. In
Java, the basis of encapsulation is the class.
2.1.3 Class and Objects
A class deﬁnes the structure and behavior (data and code) that will be shared by a set of objects.
Each object of a given class contains the structure and behavior deﬁned by the class. Thus, a class
is a template for an object, and an object is an instance of a class.
2.1.4 Data Hiding
Since a class encapsulates data and code, there are mechanisms for hiding the complexity of the
implementation inside the class. Each method or variable in a class may be marked private or public.
The public interface of a class represents everything that external users of the class can access. The
private methods and data can only be accessed by code that is a member of the class. Therefore,
any other code that is not a member of the class cannot access a private method or variable. Hence,
data is protected from improper action.

7. Multi-threaded Programming
7.1 Introduction
Java supports multithreaded programming. A multithreaded program contains two or more parts
that can run concurrently. Each part of such a program is called a thread , and each thread has a
separate path of execution.
A process is a program under execution. Process-based multitasking is the feature that allows
computer to run two or more programs concurrently. In process-based multitasking, a program is
the smallest unit of code that can be dispatched by the scheduler.
•In a thread-based multitasking environment, the thread is the smallest unit of dispatchable
code. Hence, a single program can perform two or more tasks simultaneously.
• Multitasking threads require less overhead than multitasking processes.
•Multithreading provides ability to write efﬁcient programs that make maximum use of the
processing power available in the system.
A thread can exists in different states.
• A thread can be running .
• A thread can be ready to run as soon as it gets CPU time.
•A running thread can be suspended , which temporarily halts its activity. A suspended thread
can then be resumed, allowing it to pick up where it left off.
• A thread can be blocked when waiting for a resource.
• At any time, a thread can be terminated , which halts its execution immediately.
7.1.1 Thread Priorities
Each thread is assigned a priority. Thread priorities are integers that specify the relative priority of
one thread to another. A thread’s priority is used to decide when to switch from one running thread
to the next. This is called a context switch .
•A thread can voluntarily relinquish control. In this scenario, the highest-priority thread
among the threads, ready to run, is given the CPU.
•A thread can be preempted by a higher-priority thread. As soon as a higher-priority thread
wants to run, it does. This is called preemptive multitasking.
